basics.name: DIN 8593 'Fertigungsverfahren Fügen' (Manufacturing processes: joining), parts 0 to 8, plus the withdrawn 1984 draft part 9 (textile joining)
basics.url: https://www.dinmedia.de/en/standard/din-8593-0/65031206 (DIN Media page for Part 0, the overview part; opened). Free German summary of the whole tree: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCgen_(Fertigungstechnik)
basics.resource_type: classification system (German national standard in 9 parts; a process taxonomy that sits under main group 4 'Fügen' of the DIN 8580 manufacturing-process system)
basics.cost: Paid, bought one part at a time from DIN Media. Part 0 costs 36.70 EUR as a PDF or 47.20 EUR in print. Parts 1, 3 and 4 cost 52.20 EUR each, and parts 6, 7 and 8 cost 36.70 EUR each (PDF, VAT included). Resellers sell Part 0 for about 46 USD (en-standard.eu). The full set of 9 current parts comes to roughly 380 to 410 EUR; prices for parts 2 and 5 were not checked [uncertain]
basics.license: All rights reserved (DIN standards are copyrighted and sold under licence; reproduction is not allowed). The group names, numbers and short definitions can be cited as facts. The free German Wikipedia summaries are CC BY-SA 4.0 (licence link in the page footer), so they can be quoted or adapted with attribution and share-alike
basics.language: German. The standard's original language is German, and DIN Media gives only English titles (e.g. 'Manufacturing processes joining - Part 1: Assembling'). No official English translation was found [uncertain]
basics.year: First published as the single standard DIN 8593:1967-12 (12 pages, now withdrawn). Split into parts 0 to 8 in September 1985. Current edition 2003-09 for all parts; a textile-joining part 9 only ever reached a 1984-06 draft, which was withdrawn. DIN's terminology committee scheduled the DIN 8593 series for review in 2024 (DIN-Mitteilungen 2024-01), but no new edition had appeared by 2026 [uncertain]. The parent standard DIN 8580 was revised in 2022-12
basics.access_barrier: paywall (each part must be bought; no free official text). Free overviews on German Wikipedia and German teaching sites
basics.image_license: The standard's own figures are all rights reserved (whether each part has explanatory sketches is not verified [uncertain]). The German Wikipedia articles on the groups have almost no diagrams (the Fügen article shows only the DIN logo). DIN's own news page shows overview figures (Bild 1 to 3), which are also all rights reserved
basics.authority_level: official standard (DIN, German Institute for Standardization; committee NA 152-06-10 AA 'Terminologie der Fertigungsverfahren')

coverage.covers: Every way of permanently or detachably joining solid parts (the 'Fügen' main group of manufacturing processes). There are 9 groups: 4.1 assembling (Zusammensetzen): lay on, insert, slide into each other, hook in, twist-lock (bayonet) and spring in (snap fits, clips, retaining rings). 4.2 filling (Füllen): e.g. impregnating, and filling gaps with lead, casting resin or foam. 4.3 pressing on and pressing in (Anpressen, Einpressen): screwing, clamping, clipping with staples, press fits and crimping, nailing and powder-actuated stud setting, wedging, bracing. 4.4 joining by primary forming (Fügen durch Urformen): casting in, embedding, overmoulding, potting, vulcanising in, electroforming in, sheathing, cementing with putty (Kitten). 4.5 joining by forming (Fügen durch Umformen): notching, centre-punching, collar joining, expanding, spreading, narrowing, necking, flanging, seaming, bending, tab joining (Verlappen), riveting and clinching, plus wire methods (twisting, stranding, splicing, knotting, weaving, stitching). 4.6 welding. 4.7 soldering and brazing. 4.8 adhesive bonding (Kleben). 4.9 textile joining (sewing, weaving, knitting, braiding, felting). DIN says the series defines almost 100 individual joining processes, 'from A for Auflegen via N for Nageln to Z for Zwischenzapfennieten'
coverage.organisation: A strict numbered hierarchy by manufacturing process: main group 4 (joining) → group 4.x → process 4.x.y, going down to a fifth level in places. Grouping is by how the joint is made (by putting parts together, by elastic pressure, by casting, by deforming, by melting, with solder, with glue, with textiles), not by what the joint has to do. For beginners it's mixed: the group 4.1 verbs are plain and easy to picture (lay on, insert, slide in, hook in, twist in, spring in), but the rest assumes you already know the process names, and everything is in German
coverage.scope_match: low: it's a manufacturing-process taxonomy, not a catalogue of clever connection or mechanism TYPES. It has no mechanisms, gear trains, powered connectors or special behaviours, and much of it (welding, soldering, riveting, screwing) is standard joining. It's still useful as an authoritative backbone for the joining side of the project, and group 4.1 names several in-scope types (bayonet/twist-lock, snap fit, clip, retaining ring, spring hook-in)
coverage.taxonomy_used: DIN 8580 ordinal system: main group 4 'Fügen' split into 9 groups (4.1 Zusammensetzen, 4.2 Füllen, 4.3 Anpressen/Einpressen, 4.4 Fügen durch Urformen, 4.5 Fügen durch Umformen, 4.6 Fügen durch Schweißen, 4.7 Fügen durch Löten, 4.8 Kleben, 4.9 Textiles Fügen), each subdivided in its own part (DIN 8593-1 to -8). For example, 4.1 has 6 processes (4.1.1 lay on/set on; 4.1.2 lay in/insert; 4.1.3 slide into each other; 4.1.4 hook in; 4.1.5 twist-lock (Einrenken); 4.1.6 spring in (federnd Einspreizen)), and 4.3 has 7 (screwing, clamping, stapling/clipping, press fitting, nailing/driving in, wedging, bracing). The German Wikipedia article also gives two cross-cutting schemes from general joining practice (not from DIN 8593 itself): by how it holds (shape: Formschluss, friction: Kraftschluss, material bond: Stoffschluss) and by whether it comes apart (detachable, conditionally detachable, permanent)
coverage.example_types: bayonet / twist-lock joint (Einrenken: push then turn, held by shape, released by overcoming friction or a spring, passing a detent step or opening a lock); snap-fit joint (Schnappverbindung, under 'federnd Einspreizen'); clip joint (Clipverbindung); retaining ring / circlip and expanding ring (Sicherungsring, Spreizring); leaf-spring clip (Blechfeder); hooking into a tension spring (Einhängen, e.g. tailgate hinges); sliding or telescoping fit (Ineinanderschieben, with clearance or transition fit); wedge joint (Verkeilen, self-locking); clamping joint (Klemmen); press / interference fit (Pressverbindung) and crimp joint (Crimpverbindung); powder-actuated stud setting (Bolzensetzen); clinching (Durchsetzfügen); sheet-metal seaming (Falzen) and flanging (Bördeln); tab bending / lanced tabs (Verlappen); collar joining (Kragenfügen); wire twisting, splicing and knotting; overmoulding and insert moulding (Umspritzen, Einbetten); potting and casting in (Vergießen, Eingießen); adhesive bonding (Kleben); sewing (textile joining)
coverage.making_methods: Industrial manufacturing and assembly in general: metalworking, sheet metal, casting, plastics processing, electronics and textiles. Not aimed at 3D printing, and 3D printing is not a joining group (DIN 8580:2022 added additive manufacturing as group 1.10 under primary forming, not under joining)
coverage.item_count: 9 groups (8 current parts plus the withdrawn textile draft); almost 100 individual joining processes defined, down to a fifth level in places (DIN news page). The Wikipedia summaries list 6 processes in 4.1, 7 in 4.3, 9 in 4.4, and 13 sheet/solid processes plus about 7 wire processes in 4.5
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Mostly not covered, because the scheme classifies how a joint is made, not how it behaves. Self-locking: only wedging (Verkeilen), described on Wikipedia as a self-locking (selbsthemmend) connection. Indexing/detent and hand-release: partly, since the definition of Einrenken (twist-lock) mentions release by overcoming friction or a spring force, passing a detent step (Raststufe) or opening a lock. Compliant: partly, via 'federnd Einspreizen' (snap fits and clips work by elastic deflection). Torque-limiting, one-way/ratchet, over-centre, print-in-place, gear trains and powered connectors: no. Adhesive types: adhesive bonding is its own part (DIN 8593-8), but its subdivision was not seen (probably by how the adhesive sets rather than by chemistry for each material [uncertain]), and it's not a guide to choosing an adhesive for a material
coverage.entry_structure: Each process has an ordinal number, a German term and a short definition, with some explanatory notes and examples. Whether the parts include sketches was not verified [uncertain]. The free Wikipedia versions give a paragraph and everyday examples per process (e.g. spare wheel in its well for 'insert', camera lenses and BNC plugs for 'twist-lock')
coverage.audience_level: professional (manufacturing and design engineers, standards users); widely taught in German vocational training and undergraduate manufacturing courses

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low: German only, paywalled, and terse definitions for specialists. The free Wikipedia and teaching-site summaries (e.g. technikermathe.de) are much friendlier and give everyday examples, but they are still in German
usefulness.has_images: Uncertain for the standard itself [uncertain]. The free German Wikipedia articles are text-only. DIN's news page shows an overview chart of the group 4 tree (Bild 2, taken from DIN 8580:2022-12 Bild 5). German teaching sites add their own photos
usefulness.gaps: No mechanisms, motion or adjustable connections. No special behaviours (torque limiting, one-way, over-centre, hand-release). Nothing for 3D printing or print-in-place. No design rules, pictures or selection help. Adhesives are classified as a process, not by chemistry and material. Everything is in German and behind a paywall. The 2003 terms predate modern maker techniques (heat-set inserts, printed snap fits, magnets) and powered latches
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Partly. DIN Media has stable per-part product URLs (e.g. https://www.dinmedia.de/en/standard/din-8593-1/65031218 for Part 1, assembling), but they are sales pages. German Wikipedia has one article per group (e.g. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCgen_(Fertigungstechnik) with links to Zusammensetzen, An- und Einpressen, Fügen durch Umformen, etc.). These are fine as 'official classification' links for the German name, but useless for most English readers
usefulness.reusable_data: No dataset. The tree (numbers and names) is short enough to rebuild by hand from the Wikipedia summaries, and names and numbers are facts that can be cited. The standard's definitions are copyrighted, so don't copy them; the Wikipedia wording is CC BY-SA 4.0 (attribution and share-alike)
usefulness.maintained: Current edition 2003-09 for parts 0 to 8, listed as [CURRENT] on DIN Media in 2026. DIN reviews standards at least every 5 years, and the series was put up for review in 2024; whether a revision followed is unknown [uncertain]. The German Wikipedia Fügen article was last edited on 30 April 2024
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) The plain assembly-motion verbs of group 4.1 (lay on, insert, slide in, hook in, twist-lock, spring in) make an excellent beginner flow-chart question: 'How do the parts go together?'. (2) The three holding principles, held by shape (Formschluss), friction (Kraftschluss) or material bond (Stoffschluss), as a top-level filter. (3) The detachable / conditionally detachable / permanent split as a filter (it maps to the project's removability field). (4) Stable numbered codes (4.1.5 etc.) as a cross-reference column so entries can cite the official German process name. (5) The idea of 'auxiliary joining parts' (Hilfsfügeteile: screws, rivets, staples, wedges) vs joining the parts directly, to separate hardware-based from integral connections
usefulness.design_rules_given: No. It gives terminology and classification only, with no dimensions, clearances or strengths
usefulness.file_formats: PDF download or printed copy (each part is 4 to 6 pages)
usefulness.terminology_value: high for German names and their English equivalents: Einrenken = bayonet/twist-lock joining, federnd Einspreizen = snap-in/spring-in joining, Einhängen = hooking in, Ineinanderschieben = sliding together, Verkeilen = wedging, Klemmen = clamping, Pressverbindung = press/interference fit, Durchsetzfügen = clinching, Falzen = seaming, Bördeln = flanging, Verlappen = tab joining, Kleben = adhesive bonding, Fügen durch Urformen = joining by primary forming (casting/moulding in). DIN Media's official English part titles give English group names (assembling; filling; joining by mechanical means; joining by processing of amorphous materials; joining by forming; welding; soldering or brazing; adhesives)
usefulness.decision_support: None. It's a classification only, with no selector, comparison tables or flow chart. Its hierarchy could serve as the skeleton of a 'how is it joined' branch
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Sub-standard of DIN 8580 (manufacturing processes; current 2022-12 edition, whose Bild 5 shows the group 4 overview). The welding part lines up with the separate welding-process standards (DIN 1910-100 split into fusion and pressure welding) [uncertain]. The German Wikipedia 'Fügen (Fertigungstechnik)' article and its child articles are the free restatement to cite (count them with this item, not separately). Overlaps with Messler's taxonomy of joining methods (mechanical / adhesive / welding-soldering) in 'Integral Mechanical Attachment' and with the German Wikipedia article 'Verbindungstechnik'
